identity_notes: This retrieval was heavily contaminated with unrelated records sharing keyword overlap only (dozens of appendectomy-technique meta-analyses, H. pylori eradication-regimen trials, and various other surgical/clinical topics with no connection to CLA) -- these made up the large majority of the 159 screened records and were rejected as off_topic. The genuine CLA evidence base (48 kept) is a well-studied but largely disappointing/adverse picture for the isomeric CLA mixtures (50:50 or similar c9,t11/t10,c12 blends) actually sold as supplements: two linked meta-analyses on the same 18-study set found only a MODEST fat-mass reduction (17490954) and a small (<1%) fat-free-mass increase (19935864); a larger, more recent meta-analysis found CLA significantly INCREASES CRP and TNF-alpha (29288248), and another found no significant blood-pressure benefit (25889408) and no effect on fasting glucose/waist circumference (28176632); leptin meta-analyses are null overall with benefit only in narrow subgroups (29219061, 29401538). Safety signals recur across the primary-RCT literature: increased lipid peroxidation and oxidative-stress markers (10683436, 35623803), worsened endothelial function (16339498), dose-dependent liver enzyme elevation in a 12-week RCT (17898458), and a case report of CLA-induced acute liver failure requiring transplantation (38975608). A pediatric RCT (20200257) reduced body fat but also lowered HDL and bone mineral accretion versus placebo. Several records use CLA only as one component of a fixed multi-ingredient combination (calcium, creatine+whey protein, nitrate/nitrite, a goat-cheese product, a carpal-tunnel nutraceutical) and were flagged related_form_differs since CLA's own contribution cannot be isolated. Overall this identity's evidence does not support a clean 'more CLA is better' story -- the safety signals are as prominent as the efficacy signals.
